query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A pre-engineered, nanostructured reactive surface modification imposed on a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will catalyze the rapid in situ formation of a graded, self-healing oxide tribofilm during sliding, thereby maintaining a consistently low coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate across the entire temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with its as-processed microstructure lacking any specific, reactive surface engineering.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled nanostructured reactive surface modification via a preformed thin interfacial coating or precise laser surface texturing to create uniformly distributed reactive sites.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted in ambient oxygen-containing environments with continuous temperature ramping from room temperature to 800 °C under variable normal loads.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a graded, self-healing oxide tribofilm at the sliding interface that adapts its structure and composition with temperature and load.
generation.mechanism: The engineered reactive sites on the nanostructured surface accelerate in situ oxidation upon friction-induced heating, leading to a lubricious and load-bearing oxide layer that self-heals. This adaptive tribofilm minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact, reduces plastic deformation and adhesive wear, and stabilizes friction and wear behavior despite variable operational conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, the modified alloy will exhibit a consistently lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate over the full temperature range, even as load and environmental conditions vary.
generation.baseline: The standard CoCrFeNi alloy, which typically shows increased friction and wear rates under high-temperature regions and varying loads due to imperfect or unstable oxide formation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold during sliding in oxygen-rich environments at temperatures from room temperature to 800 °C and under moderate to high loads typical of tribological applications. Its effectiveness may be compromised in highly reducing atmospheres or at load/temperature extremes beyond the tested regimes.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvements in friction and wear rates are uncertain as the kinetics of oxide tribofilm formation and self-healing behavior may vary with sliding speed and load; further experimental validation is needed to define precise performance gains.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy samples: one set receiving the nanostructured reactive surface modification (implemented via a preformed thin coating or laser surface texturing) and a second, control set with no surface modification. Subject both sets to identical ball‐on‐disk sliding wear experiments with a continuous temperature ramp from room temperature to 800 °C under variable normal loads in an ambient oxygen atmosphere.
measurements: Record the coefficient of friction as a function of temperature and applied load.
Quantify wear rate (e.g., using high-resolution topographical measurements) across the temperature range.
Conduct detailed surface characterization (e.g., SEM, EDS, XRD) to verify the existence, continuity, and self-healing behavior of the oxide tribofilm on the modified surfaces.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified CoCrFeNi samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the control samples over the full temperature range and variable loads, or if a graded, self-healing oxide tribofilm is not observed to form consistently during testing, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

The figure demonstrates a discernible connection between the wear rate and load, indicating that the wear rate exhibits a positive correlation with increasing load increments. The observed correlation between the increasing load and the accelerated rate of wear in case of composite and copper matrix suggests a corresponding increase in material loss under higher loads. This increase in material loss is due to increased plastic deformation induced at the higher loading conditions during sliding. This increase in plastic deformation results in material transfer between the sliding parts, from soft material to hard material which will come out as debris. This loss of material due to plastic deformation increases higher load and hence wear rate increases.

In this study, we successfully synthesized a transition metal dichalcogenide high entropy alloy of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 with 2D structure and tested its tribological properties by performing ball‐on‐disk friction experiments using steel against steel tribopair in an ambient environment. The lubricant was coated onto the steel substrate by the conventional air spray coating process. The lubricant displayed excellent tribological properties with low average coefficient of friction (COF) and wear rates of ≈0.076 and 2.6 × 10−9 mm3 (N∙m)−1, respectively, at the high load of 9 N (contact pressure: 0.936 GPa). The analyses performed on the wear track and wear debris indicate stress‐induced tribocatalytic activity that facilitates the self‐lubricating behavior of HEA nanoflakes during friction tests performed in ambient conditions.

AbstractThe effect and mechanism of grain sizes on the tribological behavior of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) were studied by friction experiments and wear morphology analysis. Under normal low load and low sliding speed, the primary wear mechanism of the HEA samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the samples are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. The oxide layer formed under the action of friction heat of the coarse grain (CG) sample is easy to break due to the softening of the CG. With the increase of normal load and sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the HEA samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation. The oxide layer of CG sample has many cracks, and the worn surface also has plastic deformation, which leads to the increase of friction coefficient and specific wear rate and the decrease of wear resistance. Therefore, the fine grain size HEA sample has better wear resistance than the CG sample due to its high surface strength.Keywords: high entropy alloy, grain size, tribological behavior, wear mechanism

In the present study, the tribological properties of different grain sizes CoCrFeMnNi HEAs were systematically analyzed based on sliding experiments and worn surface morphology characterization under different sliding speeds and normal loads. The results can be summarized as follows: Under the normal low load and low sliding speed, the main wear mechanism of FG and CG samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. However, the material of CG is easy to soften under the action of friction heat during high sliding speed, and the oxide layer formed is easy to fracture. Under the normal high load, the wear mechanisms of FG and CG samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation with the increase of sliding speed. The oxidation layer formed on CG sample has many cracks, and the wear surface of CG sample also has plastic deformation, resulting in an increase in friction coefficient and specific wear rate and a decrease in wear resistance. Therefore, under high load and low load, FG sample has good wear resistance due to its high surface strength.

Both sliding speed and normal load will affect the friction and wear behavior of the different grain size CoCrFeMnNi HEAs. Increasing the sliding speed will increase the friction coefficient and specific wear rate of the alloy. Thus, increase the normal load, reduce the friction coefficient, and decrease the specific wear rate of the alloy. This is because the oxide layer formed on the worn surface under high load plays a role in lubrication and reduces the friction coefficient and specific wear rate.

decision.trend: Early work in high‐entropy alloy tribology has largely focused on adjusting the near‐surface microstructure. For example, studies like PMC7311485 demonstrated that refining the grain size and harnessing inverse Hall‐Petch effects can prompt dynamic surface amorphization that lowers friction. In parallel, research such as PMC8470387 used targeted alloying (e.g., adding W to an AlCoCrFeNi matrix) to generate intermetallic precipitates and enhance lattice distortion, producing phases that help reduce wear at high temperature. Both approaches, however, have only achieved low friction or wear improvements under limited conditions (e.g., vacuum or a narrow temperature window), and none have created a consistently adaptive tribolayer across the full range from room temperature to 800 °C under variable loads and environments.
decision.unsolved: There remains a lack of a single intervention that can reliably engineer the surface of a CoCrFeNi matrix to form a robust, self-healing, and adaptive tribolayer that maintains low friction and wear across a wide temperature range, despite changes in load and ambient conditions.
decision.lever: introduce a controlled, nanostructured reactive surface modification (e.g., a preformed thin interfacial coating or laser-textured surface) designed to promote the in situ formation of a graded, self-healing oxide tribofilm
decision.why: This approach leverages the trend observed in other HEA systems—namely, the use of surface engineering to trigger adaptive modifications (such as reactive wear protection and dynamic nanocrystalline glaze formation) during sliding. By pre-designing the interface to form a lubricious, stable oxide layer that is graded with temperature, this intervention addresses the fully variable operational conditions typical for CoCrFeNi alloys, and directly follows cues from prior evidence aiming for adaptive tribological performance.
